transcript:
Meeting header: date 2027-06-30 14:00 PDT, duration ~55m. Attendees: Marcus (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lena, Rahul, Karen, Derek.

[00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I want to run through the last two days of bench results and focus on the tail latencies that popped up. Is this still a good time?
[00:18] Lena: Yep this is good. We just pulled the latest. Quick note: some of the numbers are from night batch traffic and might skew throughput.
[00:32] Sofia: got it. I'll call out which runs were steady-state vs burst. We saw a couple of 95th/99th spikes around the 10k token window.
[00:45] Rahul: the spikes correlate with KV cache misses — maybe the K V cache warmup[] -- our cache hit ratio fell to about 68% for a short period.
[00:58] Ethan: interesting, did you see those on the incumbernt runs too or just on Redwood?
[01:06] Rahul: both but more pronounced on Redwood in two runs, about +35ms at p95 and +110ms at p99 vs baseline.
[01:18] Marcus: ok let's unpack. Sofia, can you summarize which configs produced the best steady-state throughput?
[01:27] Sofia: sure — the q4_0 quantized variant shaved unit cost but increased median by 5ms. The fp16 variant with aggressive batching and dynamic batching set to 64 tokens had best throughput — 420 rps on our test rig — compared to incumbent ~330 rps. But the tail was worse when cache heat was low.
[01:50] Karen: wait, so throughput is better overall but tail latency worse in cold cache scenarios? that matches our user complaints where rare slow responses break UX flows.
[02:03] Derek: yep - the issue is the long-tail timeouts in our orchestration; we have 3s frontend timeout and anything above 1.8s causes retries.
[02:14] Marcus: ok risk is real. Two levers: routing policy to prefer warm-cached instances and fallback to a quantized lower-cost variant for overloaded nodes. Also consider prefix caching at the edge — we've seen good wins.
[02:26] Lena: can you explain prefix caching? in our stack it sounds like extra infra.
[02:32] Sofia: sure. Essentially we keep hot KV cache entries for common prefixes in the serving pool. So many requests reuse a cached K V — sorry K V cash — uh K V cache entry and avoid repeated key lookup. It saves ~50-70ms on the long tail if hit ratio >80%.
[02:48] Rahul: earlier you mentioned automatic batching. Our traffic is spiky and client bursts vary - dynamic batching helps but increases per-request latency on small messages.
[02:58] Ethan: yes that's the tradeoff. We tune per-route batching thresholds; for short prompts you set smaller batch_size/latency-window. For your high-throughput route we can use continuous batching with a 8ms window to keep latency low and still aggregate.
[03:18] Marcus: let's go through a concrete experiment plan. First: enable prefix/KV cache for the top-10 prompt templates for 24h and measure p95/p99. Second: implement routing rule to prefer cached pool, otherwise fallback to q4_0 quantized variant after 900ms. Third: run 1h tail-latency test in production-like window.
[03:37] Lena: sounds reasonable. What's the risk of degraded quality with q4_0 fallback?
[03:42] Sofia: in our internal evals quality drop is small for classification and short or structured prompts, but generative open-ended tasks show divergence. We can restrict fallback to non-generative routes.
[03:54] Rahul: also need to know cost delta. If we keep a dedicated small warm pool that adds egress cost but reduces retries maybe net win.
[04:03] Marcus: I'll share a cost calc. Ethan will propose dedicated pool sizing.
[04:10] Ethan: for your current qps, a warm pool of 4 slots (A100 equivalent) should handle spikes with 99% of requests warm, keeping p99 under 400ms — rough numbers, will firm up after data.
[04:26] Karen: on security — we need to confirm VPC peering and SAML SSO support before we move to any dedicated private deployment. Also SOC2 docs.
[04:37] Marcus: yes we'll share the SOC2 and SAML design. That security deep dive is a separate session. We'll provision a stub VPC diagram.
[04:45] Derek: on deployment, our infra team needs a simple routing YAML to plug into our ingress. Any chance you can give us a sample?
[04:53] Sofia: yes, I'll send a sample routing policy snippet. It will include priority rules: prefer cached pool, then pooled capacity, then quantized fallback with a max percentage of traffic. We'll include canary weights.
[05:04] Lena: canary weights — how are rollouts controlled? we want gradual ramp and immediate rollback if latency regresses.
[05:11] Ethan: Redwood's console supports canary thresholds and automatic fallback on latency SLO breaches. We'll show a sample: start 5% -> 25% -> 50% with automated rollback at >2% error.
[05:23] Rahul: curious — what's the granularity of metrics? per-route per-token breakdown?
[05:28] Marcus: token-level breakdowns are in Console: latency by token bucket, cost per token, and traces for specific requests. We'll give you a short recording of that view.
[05:40] Marcus: ok let's look briefly at the CSV you sent — Sofia, you flagged run #17 as the worst offender. Can you walk us through the timestamps?
[05:48] Sofia: sure. run17 was at 02:20 UTC, concurrent load ramped from 120 to 420 rps in 60s. The cache hit dropped due to an upstream purge, then the p99 hit 1.6s. The baseline vendor had p99 of ~1.2s same window. So Redwood did better median but worse tail.
[06:10] Lena: was there any hardware eviction or compaction going on?
[06:14] Sofia: we saw a background compaction job in the host (noisy neighbor) affecting memory bandwidth — we annotated that in the logs. Ethan: we can try isolating the dedicated slots to prevent noisy neighbor.
[06:25] Ethan: yes, that was our test rig's hypervisor doing cleanup. In Dedicated we'd put these on isolated GPU hosts to avoid this.
[06:33] Marcus: good. So to summarize technical path: 1) enable prefix caching for top templates 2) spin up small dedicated warm pool 3) routing policy with fallback to q4_0 for specific routes 4) measure 1h tail-latency test and compare to incumbent.
[06:48] Karen: timeline?
[06:51] Marcus: Sofia will push config and CSV by 7/2; Rahul runs the 1h by 7/5; Ethan and I will send routing and cost by 7/6. Security deep dive 7/8.
[07:00] Derek: one practical Q — will enabling caching require any SDK changes on our side or just server-side config?
[07:05] Sofia: purely server side for prefix cache. But for client-side dedup you might add a small header to prefer cached responses. We'll doc that.
[07:14] Rahul: also we need to validate audit logs — if we move to dedicated we need audit trail retention for 2 years.
[07:21] Marcus: note taken. We'll include audit log retention options and an estimate.
[07:27] (cross talk) Lena: cool, thanks.
[07:30] Marcus: ok final quick Q from me — any blockers on your side to run the 1h test?
[07:34] Lena: nothing blocking, we'll pick production-like window and notify Redwood.
[07:38] Marcus: perfect. we'll follow up in the email thread with links.
[07:42] (end of main transcript).

Post-call notes: there were a few mis-transcribed technical terms (K V cache -> K V cash in auto transcript) and short crosstalk segments. Full logs and CSVs referenced in action items.
